entries.361233e4e49374b8c204fcd473f55bed4741da4e: <div sID="gen10831" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="Ps.27" sID="Ps.27"/> <div eID="gen10831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10832" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10833" type="x-p"/> Some think David penned this psalm before his coming to the throne, when he was in the midst of his troubles, and perhaps upon occasion of the death of his parents; but the Jews think he penned it when he was old, upon occasion of the wonderful deliverance he had from the sword of the giant, when Abishai succoured him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.21.16-2Sam.21.17">2 Sam. xxi. 16, 17</reference>) and his people thereupon resolved he should never venture his life again in battle, lest he should quench the light of Israel. Perhaps it was not penned upon any particular occasion; but it is very expressive of the pious and devout affections with which gracious souls are carried out towards God at all times, especially in times of trouble. Here is, I. The courage and holy bravery of his faith, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1-Ps.27.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The complacency he took in communion with God and the benefit he experienced by it, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4-Ps.27.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. III. His desire towards God, and his favour and grace, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7-Ps.27.9">ver. 7-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">12</reference>. IV. His expectations from God, and the encouragement he gives to others to hope in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">ver. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">14</reference>. And let our hearts be thus affected in singing this psalm.
entries.7057d69c2689a0846d7d1878353d517ff8407dee: <div eID="gen10833" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10832" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Confidence; Encouragement in Prayers.</title> <div sID="gen10834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? <hi type="super">2</hi> When the wicked, <hi type="italic">even</hi> mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell. <hi type="super">3</hi> Though a host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this <hi type="italic">will</hi> I <hi type="italic">be</hi> confident. <hi type="super">4</hi> One <hi type="italic">thing</hi> have I desired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to enquire in his temple. <hi type="super">5</hi> For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock. <hi type="super">6</hi> And now shall mine head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me: therefore will I offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy; I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen10834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10835" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, <div eID="gen10835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10836" type="x-p"/> I. With what a lively faith David triumphs in God, glories in his holy name, and in the interest he had in him. 1. <hi type="italic">The Lord is my light.</hi> David's subjects called him <hi type="italic">the light of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2 Sam. xxi. 17</reference>. And he was indeed a burning and a shining light: but he owns that he shone, as the moon does, with a borrowed light; what light God darted upon him reflected upon them: <hi type="italic">The Lord is my light.</hi> God is a light to his people, to show them the way when they are in doubt, to comfort and rejoice their hearts when they are in sorrow. It is in his light that they now walk on in their way, and in his light they hope to see light for ever. 2. "He is <hi type="italic">my salvation,</hi> in whom I am safe and by whom I shall be saved." 3. "He is <hi type="italic">the strength of my life,</hi> not only the protector of my exposed life, who keeps me from being slain, but the strength of my frail weak life, who keeps me from fainting, sinking, and dying away." God, who is a believer's light, is the strength of his life, not only by whom, but in whom, he lives and moves. In God therefore let us strengthen ourselves. <div eID="gen10836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10837" type="x-p"/> II. With what an undaunted courage he triumphs over his enemies; no fortitude like that of faith. If God be for him, who can be against him? <hi type="italic">Whom shall I fear? Of whom shall I be afraid?</hi> If Omnipotence be his guard, he has no cause to fear; if he knows it to be so, he has no disposition to fear. If God be his light, he fears no shades; if God be his salvation, he fears no colours. He triumphs over his enemies that were already routed, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">v. 2</reference>. His enemies came upon him, <hi type="italic">to eat up his flesh,</hi> aiming at no less and assured of that, but they fell; not, "He smote them and they fell," but, "<hi type="italic">They stumbled and fell;</hi>" they were so confounded and weakened that they could not go on with their enterprise. Thus those that came to take Christ with a word's speaking were made to stagger and fall to the ground, <reference osisRef="John.18.6">John xviii. 6</reference>. The ruin of some of the enemies of God's people is an earnest of the complete conquest of them all. And therefore, these having fallen, he is fearless of the rest: "Though they be numerous, <hi type="italic">a host</hi> of them,—though they be daring and their attempts threatening,—though they <hi type="italic">encamp against me,</hi> an army against one man,—though they wage war upon me, yet <hi type="italic">my heart shall not fear.</hi>" Hosts cannot hurt us if the Lord of hosts protect us. Nay, in this assurance that God is for me "<hi type="italic">I will be confident.</hi>" Two things he will be confident of:—1. That he shall be safe. "If God is my salvation, <hi type="italic">in the time of trouble he shall hide me;</hi> he shall set me out of danger and above the fear of it." God will not only find out a shelter for his people in distress (as he did <reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">Jer. xxxvi. 26</reference>), but he will himself be their hiding-place, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">Ps. xxxii. 7</reference>. His providence will, it may be, keep them safe; at least his grace will make them easy. His name is the strong tower into which by faith they run, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>. "<hi type="italic">He shall hide me,</hi> not in the strongholds of En-gedi (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.29">1 Sam. xxiii. 29</reference>), but <hi type="italic">in the secret of his tabernacle.</hi>" The gracious presence of God, his power, his promise, his readiness to hear prayer, the witness of his Spirit in the hearts of his people—these are the secret of his tabernacle, and in these the saints find cause for that holy security and serenity of mind in which they dwell at ease. This sets them upon a rock which will not sink under them, but on which they find firm footing for their hopes; nay, it sets them <hi type="italic">up upon a rock</hi> on high, where the raging threatening billows of a stormy sea cannot touch them; it is a rock that is <hi type="italic">higher than we,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.61.2">Ps. lxi. 2</reference>. 2. That he shall be victorious (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now shall my head be lifted up above my enemies,</hi> not only so as that they cannot reach it with their darts, but so as that I shall be exalted to bear rule over them." David here, by faith in the promise of God, triumphs before the victory, and is as sure, not only of the laurel, but of the crown, as if it were already upon his head. <div eID="gen10837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10838" type="x-p"/> III. With what a gracious earnestness he prays for a constant communion with God in holy ordinances, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">v. 4</reference>. It greatly encouraged his confidence in God that he was conscious to himself of an entire affection to God and to his ordinances, and that he was in his element when in the way of his duty and in the way of increasing his acquaintance with him. If our hearts can witness for us that we delight in God above any creature, that may encourage us to depend upon him; for it is a sign we are of those whom he protects as his own. Or it may be taken thus: He desired to dwell in the house of the Lord that there he might be safe from the enemies that surrounded him. Finding himself surrounded by threatening hosts, he does not say, "<hi type="italic">One thing have I desired,</hi> in order to my safety, that I may have my army augmented to such a number," or that I may be master of such a city or such a castle, but "<hi type="italic">that I may dwell in the house of the Lord,</hi> and then I am well." Observe, <div eID="gen10838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10839" type="x-p"/> 1. What it is he desires—<hi type="italic">to dwell in the house of the Lord.</hi> In the courts of God's house the priests had their lodgings, and David wished he had been one of them. Disdainfully as some look upon God's ministers, one of the greatest and best of kings that ever was would gladly have taken his lot, have taken his lodging, among them. Or, rather, he desires that he might duly and constantly attend on the public service of God, with other faithful Israelites, according as the duty of every day required. He longed to see an end of the wars in which he was now engaged, not that he might live at ease in his own palace, but that he might have leisure and liberty for a constant attendance in God's courts. Thus Hezekiah, a genuine son of David, wished for the recovery of his health, not that he might go up to the thrones of judgment, but that he might <hi type="italic">go up to the house of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">Isa. xxxviii. 22</reference>. Note, All God's children desire to dwell in God's house; where should they dwell else? Not to sojourn there as a wayfaring man, that turns aside to tarry but for a night, nor to dwell there for a time only, as the servant that abides not in the house for ever, but to dwell there all the days of their life; for there the Son abides ever. Do we hope that praising God will be the blessedness of our eternity? Surely them we ought to make it the business of our time. <div eID="gen10839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10840" type="x-p"/> 2. How earnestly he covets this: "This is the <hi type="italic">one thing I have desired of the Lord</hi> and which I will seek after." If he were to ask but one thing of God, this should be it; for this he had at heart more than any thing. He desired it as a good thing; he desired it of the Lord as his gift and a token of his favour. And, having fixed his desire upon this as the one thing needful, he sought after it; he continued to pray for it, and contrived his affairs so as that he might have this liberty and opportunity. Note, Those that truly desire communion with God will set themselves with all diligence to seek after it, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Prov. xviii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen10840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10841" type="x-p"/> 3. What he had in his eye in it. He would dwell in God's house, not for the plenty of good entertainment that was there, in the feasts upon the sacrifices, nor for the music and good singing that were there, but <hi type="italic">to behold the beauty of the Lord and to enquire in his temple.</hi> He desired to attend in God's courts, (1.) That he might have the pleasure of meditating upon God. He knew something of the beauty of the Lord, the infinite and transcendent amiableness of the divine being and perfections; his holiness is his beauty (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>), his goodness is his beauty, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.17">Zech. ix. 17</reference>. The harmony of all his attributes is the beauty of his nature. With an eye of faith and holy love we with pleasure behold this beauty, and observe more and more in it that is amiable, that is admirable. When with fixedness of thought, and a holy flame of devout affections, we contemplate God's glorious excellencies, and entertain ourselves with the tokens of his peculiar favour to us, this is that view of the beauty of the Lord which David here covets, and it is to be had in his ordinances, for there he manifests himself. (2.) That he might have the satisfaction of being instructed in his duty; for concerning this he would <hi type="italic">enquire in God's temple.</hi> Lord, <hi type="italic">what wilt thou have me to do?</hi> For the sake of these two things he desired that one thing, to <hi type="italic">dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of his life;</hi> for blessed are those that do so; they will be still praising him (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Ps. lxxxiv. 4</reference>), both in speaking to him and in hearing from him. Mary's sitting at Christ's feet to hear his word Christ calls the <hi type="italic">one thing needful,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the good part.</hi> <div eID="gen10841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10842" type="x-p"/> 4. What advantage he promised himself by it. Could he but have a place in God's house, (1.) There he should be quiet and easy: there troubles would not find him, for he should be hid in secret; there troubles would not reach him, for he should be set on high, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">v. 5</reference>. Joash, one of David's seed, was hidden in the house of the Lord six years, and there not only preserved from the sword, but reserved to the crown, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.3">2 Kings xi. 3</reference>. The temple was thought a safe place for Nehemiah to abscond in, <reference osisRef="Neh.6.10">Neh. vi. 10</reference>. The safety of believers however is not in the walls of the temple, but in the God of the temple and their comfort in communion with him. (2.) There he should be pleasant and cheerful: there he would offer sacrifices of joy, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">v. 6</reference>. For God's work is its own wages. There <hi type="italic">he would sing, yea, he would sing praises to the Lord.</hi> Note, Whatever is the matter of our joy ought to be the matter of our praise; and, when we attend upon God in holy ordinances, we ought to be much in joy and praise. It is for the glory of our God that we should sing in his ways; and, whenever God lifts us up above our enemies, we ought to exalt him in our praises. <hi type="italic">Thanks be to God, who always causeth us to triumph,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2 Cor. ii. 14</reference>.
entries.e20ce012d5b0ae978350e77fbaf92dc7af8731e1: <div eID="gen10842" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in Divine Goodness.</title> <div sID="gen10843" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hear, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">when</hi> I cry with my voice: have mercy also upon me, and answer me. <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">When thou saidst,</hi> Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , will I seek. <hi type="super">9</hi> Hide not thy face <hi type="italic">far</hi> from me; put not thy servant away in anger: thou hast been my help; leave me not, neither forsake me, O God of my salvation. <hi type="super">10</hi> When my father and my mother forsake me, then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will take me up. <hi type="super">11</hi> Teach me thy way, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies. <hi type="super">12</hi> Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies: for false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out cruelty. 13 <hi type="italic">I had fainted,</hi> unless I had believed to see the goodness of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the land of the living. 14 Wait on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen10843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10844" type="x-p"/> David in these verses expresses, <div eID="gen10844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10845" type="x-p"/> I. His desire towards God, in many petitions. If he cannot now go up to the house of the Lord, yet, wherever he is, he can find a way to the throne of grace by prayer. <div eID="gen10845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10846" type="x-p"/> 1. He humbly bespeaks, because he firmly believes he shall have, a gracious audience: "<hi type="italic">Hear, O Lord, when I cry,</hi> not only with my heart, but, as one in earnest, <hi type="italic">with my voice too.</hi>" He bespeaks also an answer of peace, which he expects, not from his own merit, but God's goodness: <hi type="italic">Have mercy upon me, and answer me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7">v. 7</reference>. If we pray and believe, God will graciously hear and answer. <div eID="gen10846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10847" type="x-p"/> 2. He takes hold of the kind invitation God had given him to this duty, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">v. 8</reference>. It is presumption for us to come into the presence of the King of kings uncalled, nor can we draw near with any assurance unless he <hi type="italic">hold forth to us the golden sceptre.</hi> David therefore going to pray fastens, in his thoughts, upon the call God had given him to the throne of his grace, and reverently touches, as it were, the top of the golden sceptre which was thereby held out to him. <hi type="italic">My heart said unto thee</hi> (so it begins in the original) or <hi type="italic">of</hi> thee, <hi type="italic">Seek you my face;</hi> he first revolved that, and preached that over again to himself (and that is the best preaching: it is hearing twice what God speaks once)—<hi type="italic">Thou saidst</hi> (so it may be supplied), <hi type="italic">Seek you my face;</hi> and then he returns what he had so meditated upon, in this pious resolution, <hi type="italic">Thy face, Lord, will I seek.</hi> Observe here, (1.) The true nature of religious worship; it is seeking the face of God. This it is in God's precept: <hi type="italic">Seek you my face;</hi> he would have us seek him for himself, and make his favour our chief good; and this it is in the saint's purpose and desire: "<hi type="italic">Thy face, Lord, will I seek,</hi> and nothing less will I take up with." The opening of his hand will satisfy the desire of other living things (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.16">Ps. cxlv. 16</reference>), but it is only the shining of his face that will satisfy the desire of a living soul, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>. (2.) The kind of invitation of a gracious God to this duty: <hi type="italic">Thou saidst, Seek you my face;</hi> it is not only permission, but a precept; and his commanding us to seek implies a promise of finding; for he is too kind to say, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi> God calls us to seek his face in our conversion to him and in our converse with him. He calls us, by the whispers of his Spirit to and with our spirits, to seek his face; he calls us by his word, by the stated returns of opportunities for his worship, and by special providences, merciful and afflictive. When we are foolishly making our court to lying vanities God is, in love to us, calling us in him to seek our own mercies. (3.) The ready compliance of a gracious soul with this invitation. The call is immediately returned: <hi type="italic">My heart answered, Thy face, Lord, will I seek.</hi> The call was general; "<hi type="italic">Seek you my face;</hi>" but, like David, we must apply it to ourselves, "<hi type="italic">I will seek it.</hi>" The word does us no good when we transfer it to others, and do not ourselves accept the exhortation. The call was, <hi type="italic">Seek you my face;</hi> the answer is express, <hi type="italic">Thy face, Lord, will I seek;</hi> like that (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">Jer. iii. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold, we come unto thee.</hi> A gracious heart readily echoes to the call of a gracious God, being made willing in the day of his power. <div eID="gen10847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10848" type="x-p"/> 3. He is very particular in his requests. (1.) For the favour of God, that he might not be shut out from that (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thy face, Lord, will I seek,</hi> in obedience to thy command; therefore <hi type="italic">hide not thy face from me;</hi> let me never want the reviving sense of the favour; love me, and let me know that thou lovest me; <hi type="italic">put not thy servant away in anger.</hi>" He owns he had deserved God's displeasure, but begs that, however God might correct him, he would not cast him away from his presence; for what is hell but that? (2.) For the continuance of his presence with him: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast been my help</hi> formerly, and <hi type="italic">thou are the God of my salvation;</hi> and therefore whither shall I go but to thee? <hi type="italic">O leave me not, neither forsake me;</hi> withdraw not the operations of thy power from me, for then I am helpless; withdraw not the tokens of thy good-will to me, for then I am comfortless." (3.) For the benefit of divine guidance (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Teach me thy way, O Lord!</hi> give me to understand the meaning of thy providences towards me and make them plain to me; and give me to know my duty in every doubtful case, that I may not mistake it, but may walk rightly, and that I may not do it with hesitation, but may walk surely." It is not policy, but plainness (that is, downright honesty) that will direct us into and keep us in the way of our duty. He begs to be guided <hi type="italic">in a plain path, because of his enemies,</hi> or (as the margin reads it) his <hi type="italic">observers.</hi> His enemies watched for his halting, that they may find occasion against him. Saul eyed David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1 Sam. xviii. 9</reference>. This quickened him to pray, "Lord, <hi type="italic">lead me in a plain path,</hi> that they may have nothing ill, or nothing that looks ill, to lay to my charge." (4.) For the benefit of a divine protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Deliver me not over to the will of my enemies.</hi> Lord, let them not gain their point, for it aims at my life, and no less, and in such a way as that I have no fence against them, but thy power over their consciences; for <hi type="italic">false witnesses have risen up against me,</hi> that aim further than to take away my reputation or estate, for they <hi type="italic">breathe out cruelty;</hi> it is the blood, the precious blood, they thirst after." Herein David was a type of Christ; for false witnesses rose up against him, and such as breathed out cruelty; but though he was delivered into their wicked hands, he was not delivered over to their will, for they could not prevent his exaltation. <div eID="gen10848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10849" type="x-p"/> II. He expresses his dependence upon God, <div eID="gen10849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10850" type="x-p"/> 1. That he would help and succour him when all other helps and succours failed him (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When my father and my mother forsake me,</hi> the nearest and dearest friends I have in the world, from whom I may expect most relief and with most reason, when they die, or are at a distance from me, or are disabled to help me in time of need, or are unkind to me or unmindful of me, and will not help me, when I am as helpless as ever poor orphan was that was left fatherless and motherless, then I know <hi type="italic">the Lord will take me up,</hi> as a poor wandering sheep is taken up, and saved from perishing." His time to help those that trust in him is when all other helpers fail, when it is most for his honour and their comfort. With him <hi type="italic">the fatherless find mercy.</hi> This promise has often been fulfilled in the letter of it. Forsaken orphans have been taken under the special care of the divine Providence, which has raised up relief and friends for them in a way that one would not have expected. God is a surer and better friend than our earthly parents are or can be. <div eID="gen10850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10851" type="x-p"/> 2. That in due time he should see the displays of his goodness, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">v. 13</reference>. He believed he should <hi type="italic">see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living;</hi> and, if he had not done so, he would <hi type="italic">have fainted</hi> under his afflictions. Even the best saints are subject to faint when their troubles become grievous and tedious, their spirits are overwhelmed, and their flesh and heart fail. But then faith is a sovereign cordial; it keeps them from desponding under their burden and from despairing of relief, keeps them hoping, and praying, and waiting, and keeps up in them good thoughts of God, and the comfortable enjoyment of themselves. But what was it the belief of which kept David from fainting?—<hi type="italic">that he should see the goodness of the Lord,</hi> which now seemed at a distance. Those that walk by faith in the goodness of the Lord shall in due time walk in the sight of that goodness. This he hopes to see in the land of the living, that is, (1.) In this world, that he should outlive his troubles and not perish under them. It is his comfort, not so much that he shall see the land of the living as that he shall see the goodness of God in it; for that is the comfort of all creature-comforts to a gracious soul. (2.) In the land of Canaan, and in Jerusalem where the lively oracles were. In comparison with the heathen, that were dead in sin, the land of Israel might fitly be called <hi type="italic">the land of the living;</hi> there God was known, and there David hoped to see his goodness; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.25-2Sam.15.26">2 Sam. xv. 25, 26</reference>. Or, (3.), In heaven. It is that alone that may truly be called <hi type="italic">the land of the living,</hi> where there is no more death. This earth is the land of the dying. There is nothing like the believing hope of eternal life, the foresights of that glory, and foretastes of those pleasures, to keep us from fainting under all the calamities of this present time. <div eID="gen10851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10852" type="x-p"/> 3. That in the mean time he should be strengthened to bear up under his burdens (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">v. 14</reference>); whether he says it to himself, or to his friends, it comes all to one; this is that which encourages him: <hi type="italic">He shall strengthen thy heart,</hi> shall sustain thy spirit, and then the spirit shall sustain the infirmity. In that strength, (1.) Keep close to God and to your duty. <hi type="italic">Wait on the Lord</hi> by faith, and prayer, and a humble resignation to his will; <hi type="italic">wait, I say, on the Lord;</hi> whatever you do, grow not remiss in your attendance upon God. (2.) Keep up your spirits in the midst of the greatest dangers and difficulties: <hi type="italic">Be of good courage;</hi> let your hearts be fixed, trusting in God, and your minds stayed upon him, and then let none of these things move you. Those that wait upon the Lord have reason to be of good courage.  <chapter eID="Ps.27"/> <div eID="gen10852" type="x-p"/>

entries.3d632f4ebc40df8eb80f52b81a27628817154673: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5741"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 27</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.27.1-Ps.27.14">Psa 27:1-14</reference>. With a general strain of confidence, hope, and joy, especially in God's worship, in the midst of dangers, the Psalmist introduces prayer for divine help and guidance.</title> <div sID="gen8735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5741"/><hi type="bold">1. light--</hi>is a common figure for comfort.<div eID="gen8735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8736" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strength--</hi>or, "stronghold"--affording security against all violence. The interrogations give greater vividness to the negation implied. <div eID="gen8736" type="x-p"/>
entries.be9988e8e60ecaef8be27f2736978032ac990955: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5742"/><div sID="gen8737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5742"/><hi type="bold">2. eat ... my flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.19.22">Job 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Psa 14:4</reference>). The allusion to wild beasts illustrates their rapacity.<div eID="gen8737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they stumbled--</hi>"they" is emphatic; not I, but they were destroyed. <div eID="gen8738" type="x-p"/>
entries.001f03ba73839c2d16ff015430fe947146ff4b54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5743"/><div sID="gen8739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5743"/>3. In the greatest dangers.<div eID="gen8739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in this--</hi>that is, then, in such extremity. <div eID="gen8740" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fcd309459093dc4871c7e50a54f838b3ac3d6f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5744"/><div sID="gen8741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5744"/>4-5. The secret of his confidence is his delight in communion with God (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.6">23:6</reference>), beholding the harmony of His perfections, and seeking His favor in His temple or palace; a term applicable to the tabernacle (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>). There he is safe (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.21">Psa 31:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.5">61:5</reference>). The figure is changed in the last clause, but the sentiment is the same. <div eID="gen8741" type="x-p"/>
entries.4173d589abd32c7948303c458e256a3830fd5c5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5745"/><div sID="gen8742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5745"/><hi type="bold">6. head be lifted up--</hi>I shall be placed beyond the reach of my enemies. Hence he avows his purpose of rendering joyful thank offerings. <div eID="gen8742" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ec179d072dc4f15028dbba975e2cee6d71e315e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5746"/><div sID="gen8743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5746"/>7. Still pressing need extorts prayer for help.<div eID="gen8743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry with my voice--</hi>denotes earnestness. Other things equal, Christians in earnest pray audibly, even in secret. <div eID="gen8744" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7c916b2bb770d13134d1b80505c7d27bc8b59c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5747"/><div sID="gen8745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5747"/>8. The meaning is clear, though the construction in a literal translation is obscure. The English Version supplies the implied clause. To seek God's face is to seek His favor (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.4">Psa 105:4</reference>). <div eID="gen8745" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fcc2735053d21d46c3a5bbf2e7becb6ad1d44d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5748"/><div sID="gen8746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5748"/><hi type="bold">9. Hide not, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.24">22:24</reference>). Against rejection he pleads former mercy and love. <div eID="gen8746" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b36a8df00434a1ec83ef9dea8e4bc4d81b1ac21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5749"/><div sID="gen8747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5749"/>10. In the extremity of earthly destitution (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">38:11</reference>), God provides (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.25.35">Mt 25:35</reference>). <div eID="gen8747" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e445511ef628ee26af1d9579faa82f1cfa8a347: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5750"/><div sID="gen8748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5750"/><hi type="bold">11. thy way--</hi>of providence.<div eID="gen8748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a plain path--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.26.12">Psa 26:12</reference>).<div eID="gen8749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enemies--</hi>literally, "watchers for my fall" (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen8750" type="x-p"/>
entries.997e4b5c7c7785b003c25feaadfbbf8f14e0ea38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5751"/><div sID="gen8751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5751"/><hi type="bold">12. will--</hi>literally, "soul," "desire" (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.25">Psa 35:25</reference>).<div eID="gen8751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enemies--</hi>literally, "oppressors." Falsehood aids cruelty against him.<div eID="gen8752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breathe out--</hi>as being filled with it (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.1">Ac 9:1</reference>). <div eID="gen8753" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f472e7bcddcda0f5d564b14425c0a7fad1334c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5752"/><div sID="gen8754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5752"/>13. The strong emotion is indicated by the incomplete sentence, for which the English Version supplies a proper clause; or, omitting that, and rendering, "yet I believed," &c., the contrast of his faith and his danger is expressed.<div eID="gen8754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to see--</hi>is to experience (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.17">Psa 22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen8755" type="x-p"/>
entries.23c4b6f9e348fa55b2a4ac166c76b178be6c2b30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5753"/><div sID="gen8756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5753"/><hi type="bold">14. Wait, &c.--</hi>in confident expectation. The last clause is, literally, "and wait," &c., as if expecting new measures of help. <chapter eID="Ps.27"/>

entries.f6246f3d88df6f09b90cc671341f40deb9974be8: <div eID="gen19372" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19373" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19374" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19374" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19373" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19375" type="x-p"/> The righteous man's confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.27.1-Psa.27.3">Psa 27:1-3</reference>; his ardent desire to have the spiritual privilege of worshipping God in his temple, because of the spiritual blessings which he expects to enjoy there, <reference osisRef="Psa.27.4-Psa.27.6">Psa 27:4-6</reference>; his prayer to God for continual light and salvation, <reference osisRef="Psa.27.7-Psa.27.9">Psa 27:7-9</reference>; has confidence that, though even has ohm parents might forsake him, yet God would not, <reference osisRef="Psa.27.10">Psa 27:10</reference>. Therefore he begs to be taught the right way to be delivered from all his enemies, and to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living, <reference osisRef="Psa.27.11-Psa.27.13">Psa 27:11-13</reference>; he exhorts others to trust in God; to be of good courage; and to expect strength for their hearts, <reference osisRef="Psa.27.14">Psa 27:14</reference>. <div eID="gen19375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19376" type="x-p"/> In the Hebrew and Chaldee this Psalm has no other title than simply לדוד ledavid: To or For David. In the Syriac: "For David; on account of an infirmity which fell upon him." In the Vulgate, Septuagint, Arabic, and Ethiopic, it has this title: "A Psalm of David, before he was anointed." The Anglo-Saxon omits all the titles. For this title there is no authority in fact. However, it may be just necessary to state that David appears to have received the royal unction three times: <div eID="gen19376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19377" type="x-p"/> 1. In Bethlehem from the hand of Samuel, in the house of his father Jesse; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sam 16:13</reference>. <div eID="gen19377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19378" type="x-p"/> 2. At Hebron after the death of Saul, by the men of Judah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.4">2Sam 2:4</reference>. <div eID="gen19378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19379" type="x-p"/> 3. By the elders of Israel, at Hebron, after the death of Ishbosheth, when he was acknowledged king over all the tribes; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.3">2Sam 5:3</reference>. <div eID="gen19379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19380" type="x-p"/> At which of these anointings the Psalm was written, or whether before any of them, we know not; nor is the question to be decided. Some commentators say that it is a Psalm belonging to the captivity, and upon that system it may be well interpreted. And lastly, it has been contended that it was written by David after he had been in danger of losing his life by the hand of a gigantic Philistine, and must have perished had he not been succoured by Abishai; see the account <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sam 21:17</reference> (note); and was counselled by his subjects not to go out to battle any more, lest he should extinguish the light of Israel. To these advisers he is supposed to make the following reply: - <div eID="gen19380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19381" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19382" type="x-p"/> The Lord is my light and my salvation - This light can never be extinguished by man; the Lord is my salvation, my safeguard, my shield, and my defense; of whom then should I be afraid?
entries.f6357cbd02c35193a40fd03cf06391e9711054f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19383" type="x-p"/> When the wicked - came upon me - Near as I appeared to you to be in danger of losing my life, I was safe enough in the hands of the Lord; and those who thought to have eaten me up, stumbled, failed of their purpose and fell; the Philistine lost his own life.
entries.492530e3930e4fb99957822e83e2d1fde3a154ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19384" type="x-p"/> Though a host should encamp against me - I am so confident of the Almighty's protection, that were I alone, and encompassed by a host, I would not fear. I am in the hand of God; and while in that hand, I am safe.
entries.5bb187137b4db532200f5f8dc4d998085799f291: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19385" type="x-p"/> One thing have I desired - If I am grown too old, and from that circumstance unable to serve my country, I shall then prefer a retirement to the tabernacle, there to serve God the rest of my days. There I shall behold his glory, and there I may inquire and get important answers respecting Israel. <div eID="gen19385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19386" type="x-p"/> But though these words may be thus interpreted, on the above supposition, that David penned the Psalm on the occasion of his escape from the Philistine, and the desire expressed by his subjects that he should go no more out to war; yet it appears that they more naturally belong to the captivity, and that this verse especially shows the earnest longing of the captives to return to their own land, that they might enjoy the benefit of Divine worship.
entries.48be23da98be8ce6c82bb4902f11a8893c86bc68: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19387" type="x-p"/> He shall hide me in his pavilion - בסכה besuccoh, in his tabernacle. I would make his temple my residence; I would dwell with God, and be in continual safety. Pavilion comes from papilio and παπιλιων, a butterfly. It signifies a tent made of cloth stretched out on poles, which in form resembles in some measure the insect above named. <div eID="gen19387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19388" type="x-p"/> In the secret of his tabernacle - Were there no other place, he would put me in the holy of holies, so that an enemy would not dare to approach me. <div eID="gen19388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19389" type="x-p"/> He shall set me upon a rock - He shall so strengthen and establish me, that my enemies shall not be able to prevail against me. He shall hide me where they cannot find me, or put me out of the reach of the fiery darts of the wicked. He who lives nearest to God suffers least from temptation. "Draw nigh to God and he will draw nigh to thee: resist the devil and he will flee from thee."
entries.ae4e4328004b1cc284f1dc4098914cd0c6dd60df: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19390" type="x-p"/> Now shall mine head be lifted up - We shall most assuredly be redeemed from this captivity, and restored to our own land, and to the worship of our God in his own temple. There shall we offer sacrifices of joy; we will sing praises unto the Lord, and acknowledge that it is by his might and mercy alone that we have been delivered.
entries.4bcbae841c23b62bc2cc6de1a6174492c88f14bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19391" type="x-p"/> Hear, O Lord, when I cry - This is the utmost that any man of common sense can expect - to be heard when he cries. But there are multitudes who suppose God will bless them whether they cry or not; and there are others and not a few, who although they listlessly pray and cry not, yet imagine God must and will hear them! God will answer them that pray and cry; those who do not are most likely to be without the blessings which they so much need.
entries.78dafabf35850499e89d8c2f7e96e3a278c55bca: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19392" type="x-p"/> When thou saidst, Seek ye my face - How much labor and skill have been employed to make sense of this verse as it stands in our translation! The original words are the following, from which our Version has been forcibly extracted: - לך אמר לבי בקשו פני את פניך יהוה אבקש lecha amar libbi bakkeshu panai; eth paneycha, Yehovah, abakkesh; of which I believe the true rendering to be as follows: "Unto thee, my heart, he hath said, Seek ye my face. Thy face, O Jehovah, I will seek. O my heart, God hath commanded thee to seek his face." Then, his face I will seek. Which may be paraphrased thus: Unto thee, his Church, God hath said Seek ye, all who compose it, my face. To which I, his Church, have answered, Thy face, O Jehovah, I will seek. On referring to Archbishop Secker, I find that he, and indeed Bishop Horsley, are of the same mind. <div eID="gen19392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19393" type="x-p"/> I had formerly proposed another method of reading this difficult verse. Suspecting that some error had got into the text, for בקשו פני bakkeshu panay, "seek ye my face," I had substituted אבקש פניך abakkesh paneycha, "I will seek thy face;" or with the Vulgate and Septuagint, בקשתי פניך bakkesti paneycha, "I have sought thy face," exquisivit te facies mea, Εξεζητησα το προσωπον σου. And this small alteration seemed to make a good sense: "My heart said unto thee, I have sought thy face, (or, I will seek thy face), and thy face, O Lord, I will seek." I have not only done what it was my duty and interest to do, but I will continue to do it. Some have proposed to mend the text thus: לך לך אמר לבי lech lecha, amar libbi, "Go to, saith my heart," נבקש פני יהוה nebakkesh peney Jehovah, "Let us seek the face of Jehovah." This is rather a violent emendation, and is supported by neither MSS. nor Versions. The whole verse is wanting in one of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. On the whole I prefer what is first proposed, and which requires no alteration in the text; next, that of the Vulgate and Septuagint. <div eID="gen19393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19394" type="x-p"/> The old Psalter paraphrases thus: Til yhe saide my hert, the my face soght: thy face, lord, I sal seke. "The gernyng of my hert that spekes til god, and he anely heres: saide til the my face, that es my presence soght the and na nother thyng. And fra now I sal seke thy face lastandly, til my dede; and that I fynd my sekyng:" i.e., To thee, said my heart; thee my face sought: thy face, O Lord, I shall seek. The gerning of my hert, that spekes til God, and he anely heres, "til the my face"; that es, my presence soght the and no nother thyng: and fra now I sal seke thy face lastandly, til my dede, and that I fynd my sekyng:" i.e., The yearning strong desire of my heart, which speaks to God, and he alone hears; my face is to thee; that is, myself sought thee, and none other thing, and from now I shall seek thee lastingly till my death, and till that I find what I seek.
entries.c3033c60cf0b691e183bdd3a5c20cc610bbd2d53: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19395" type="x-p"/> Hide not thy face - from me - As my face is towards thee wheresoever I am, so let thy face be turned towards me. In a Persian MS. poem entitled Shah we Gudda, "The King and the Beggar," I have found a remarkable couplet, most strangely and artificially involved, which expresses exactly the same sentiment one meaning of which is: - <div eID="gen19395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19396" type="x-p"/> Our face is towards Thee in all our ways; <div eID="gen19396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19397" type="x-p"/> Thy face is towards us in all our intentions. <div eID="gen19397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19398" type="x-p"/> Something similar, though not the same sentiment is in Hafiz, lib. i., gaz. v., cap. 2: - <div eID="gen19398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19399" type="x-p"/> How can we with the disciples turn our face towards the kaaba, <div eID="gen19399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19400" type="x-p"/> When our spiritual instructer turns his face to wards the wine-cellar? <div eID="gen19400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19401" type="x-p"/> I shall subjoin a higher authority than either: - Ὁτι οφθαλμοι Κυριου επι δικαιους, Και ωτα αυτου εις δεησις αυτων· Προσωπον δε Κυριου επι ποιουντας κακα. <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.12">1Pet 3:12</reference>. <div eID="gen19401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19402" type="x-p"/> For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous; And his ears to their supplication: And the face of the Lord is upon the workers of evil.
entries.2f810109cf6e1669931a4a091d8fb017e8d0ceda: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19403" type="x-p"/> When my father and my mother forsake me - Or, more literally, "For my father and my mother have forsaken me; but the Lord hath gathered me up." My parents were my protectors for a time; but the Lord has been my Protector always. There is no time in which I do not fall under his merciful regards.
entries.7c2946bf66a56805c3e3abe580677ee0bfac7644: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19404" type="x-p"/> Teach me thy way - Let me know the gracious designs of thy providence towards me, that my heart may submit to thy will. <div eID="gen19404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19405" type="x-p"/> And lead me in a plain path - In the path of righteousness, because of mine enemies, who watch for my halting.
entries.e2081e58a62bb98da634a7bbefb16cf5e2e3d8dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19406" type="x-p"/> Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies - To their soul בנפש benephesh; their whole soul thirsts for my destruction. Let them not be gratified. They have suborned witnesses against me, but they are false witnesses: unmask their wickedness, and confound their counsels.
entries.59cdcad0f04e2125be4fd5dee281642017969664: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19407" type="x-p"/> I had fainted, unless I had believed - The words in italics are supplied by our translators; but, far from being necessary, they injure the sense. Throw out the words I had fainted, and leave a break after the verse, and the elegant figure of the psalmist will be preserved: "Unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living" - What! what, alas! should have become of me! <div eID="gen19407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19408" type="x-p"/> Dr. Hammond has observed that there is a remarkable elegance in the original, which, by the use of the beautiful figure aposiopesis, makes an abrupt breaking off in the midst of a speech. He compares it to the speech of Neptune to the winds that had raised the tempest to drown the fleet of Aeneas - Aeneid. lib. i., ver. 131. <div eID="gen19408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19409" type="x-p"/> Eurum ad se zephyrumque vocat: dehinc talia fatur; <div eID="gen19409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19410" type="x-p"/> Tantane vos generis tenuit fiducia vestri? <div eID="gen19410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19411" type="x-p"/> Jam coelum terramque, meo sine numine, venti, <div eID="gen19411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19412" type="x-p"/> Miscere, et tantas audetis tollere moles? <div eID="gen19412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19413" type="x-p"/> Quos ego-sed motos praestat componere fluctus. <div eID="gen19413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19414" type="x-p"/> To Eurus and the western blast he cried, <div eID="gen19414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19415" type="x-p"/> Does your high birth inspire this boundless pride? <div eID="gen19415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19416" type="x-p"/> Audacious winds! without a power from me, <div eID="gen19416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19417" type="x-p"/> To raise at will such mountains on the sea? <div eID="gen19417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19418" type="x-p"/> Thus to confound heaven, earth, the air, and main; <div eID="gen19418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19419" type="x-p"/> Whom I - but, first, I'll calm the waves again. <div eID="gen19419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19420" type="x-p"/> Pitts.
entries.16b1ef46cb27ffdeaf451f602c16daab1729c0c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19421" type="x-p"/> Wait on the Lord - All ye who are in distress, wait on the Lord. Take me for an example. I waited on him, and he strengthened my heart; wait ye on him, and he will strengthen your heart. You cannot be unsuccessful; fear not. Wait, I say, on the Lord; wait for his succor in doing his will. Age viriliter, says the Vulgate; act like a man, hope, believe, work, and fear not.  <chapter eID="Ps.27"/> <div eID="gen19421" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e2f6086d9c880342f2c77878531b7c18c32fc52: <div eID="gen9332" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Taking Heart in God, the All-Recompensing One</title> <div sID="gen9333" type="x-p"/> The same longing after Zion meets us sounding forth from this as from the preceding Psalm. To remain his whole life long in the vicinity of the house of God, is here his only prayer; and that, rescued from his enemies, he shall there offer sacrifices of thanksgiving, is his confident expectation. The היכל of God, the King, is at present only a אהל which, however, on account of Him who sits enthroned therein, may just as much be called היכל as the היכל which Ezekiel beheld in remembrance of the Mosaic tabernacle, אהל, Eze 41:1. Cut off from the sanctuary, the poet is himself threatened on all sides by the dangers of war; but he is just as courageous in God as in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>, where the battle is already going on: “<hi type="italic">I do not fear the myriads of people, who are encamped against me.</hi>” The situation, therefore, resembles that of David during the time of Absolom. But this holds good only of the first half, Psa 27:1. In the second half, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Psa 27:10</reference> is not in favour of its being composed by David. In fact the two halves are very unlike one another. They form a <hi type="italic">hysteron-proteron</hi>, inasmuch as the <hi type="italic">fides triumphans</hi> of the first part changes into <hi type="italic">fides supplex</hi> in the second, and with the beginning of the δέησις in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7">Psa 27:7</reference>, the style becomes heavy and awkward, the strophic arrangement obscure, and even the boundaries of the lines of the verses uncertain; so that one is tempted to regard <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7">Psa 27:7</reference> as the appendage of another writer. The compiler, however, must have had the Psalm before him exactly as we now have it; for the grounds for his placing it to follow <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1-Ps.26.12">Psa 26:1-12</reference> are to be found in both portions, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7">Psa 27:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.26.11">Psa 26:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference> with Psa 26:12.
entries.d3b8ca86761e83d6821e48ec64c19dc5cd0120f9: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1-Ps.27.3">Psa 27:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9334" type="x-p"/> In this first strophe is expressed the bold confidence of faith. It is a hexastich in the caesural schema. Let darkness break in upon him, the darkness of night, of trouble, and of spiritual conflict, yet Jahve is his Light, and if he is in Him, he is in the light and there shines upon him a sun, that sets not and knows no eclipse. This sublime, infinitely profound name for God, אורי, is found only in this passage; and there is only one other expression that can be compared with it. viz., בּא אורך in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">Isa 60:1</reference>; cf. φῶς ἐλήλυθα, Joh 12:46. ישׁעי does not stand beside אורי as an unfigurative, side by side with a figurative expression; for the statement that God is light, is not a metaphor. David calls Him his “salvation” in regard to everything that oppresses him, and the “stronghold (מעוז from עזז, with an unchangeable <hi type="italic">å</hi>) of his life” in regard to everything that exposes him to peril. In Jahve he conquers far and wide; in Him his life is hidden as it were behind a fortress built upon a rock (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference>). When to the wicked who come upon him in a hostile way (קרב על differing from קרב אל), he attributes the intention of devouring his flesh, they are conceived of as wild beasts. To eat up any one’s flesh signifies, even in <reference osisRef="Job.19.22">Job 19:22</reference>, the same as to pursue any one by evil speaking (in Aramaic by slander, back-biting) to his destruction. In בּקרב (the <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi> of the only faintly closed syllable is raised to a <hi type="italic">Chateph</hi>, as in ולשׁכני, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>, לשׁאול, and the like. The לי of איבי לּי may, as also in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>), be regarded as giving intensity to the notion of special, personal enmity; but a mere repetition of the subject (the enemy) without the repetition of their hostile purpose would be tame in the parallel member of the verse: לי is a variation of the preceding עלי, as in Lam 3:60. In the apodosis המּה כּשׁלוּ ונפלוּ, the overthrow of the enemy is regarded beforehand as an accomplished fact. The holy boldness and imperturbable repose are expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.3">Psa 27:3</reference> in the very rhythm. The thesis or downward movement in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.27.3">Psa 27:3</reference></hi> is spondaic: he does not allow himself to be disturbed; the thesis in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.27.3">Psa 27:3</reference></hi> is iambic: he can be bold. The rendering of Hitzig (as of Rashi): “in this do I trust, viz., that Jahve is my light, etc.,” is erroneous. Such might be the interpretation, if בזאת אני בוטח closed <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference>; but it cannot refer back over <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>; and why should the poet have expressed himself thus materially, instead of saying ביהוה? The fact of the case is this, בוטח signifies even by itself “of good courage,” e.g., <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; and בזאת “in spite of this” (Coccejus: <hi type="italic">hoc non obstante</hi>), <reference osisRef="Lev.26.27">Lev 26:27</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.32">Psa 78:32</reference>, begins the apodosis, at the head of which we expect to find an adversative conjunction.
entries.4f2bf4a9b15045f25e9b855d12a1cb0c2e0f568a: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4-Ps.27.5">Psa 27:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen9334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9335" type="x-p"/> There is only one thing, that he desires, although he also has besides full satisfaction in Jahve in the midst of strangers and in trouble. The future is used side by side with the perfect in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Psa 27:4</reference></hi>, in order to express an ardent longing which extends out of the past into the future, and therefore runs through his whole life. The one thing sought is unfolded in שׁבתּי וגו. A life-long dwelling in the house of Jahve, that is to say intimate spiritual intercourse with the God, who has His dwelling (בית), His palace (היכל) in the holy tent, is the one desire of David’s heart, in order that he may behold and feast upon (חזה בּ of a clinging, lingering, chained gaze, and consequently a more significant form of expression than חזה with an accusative, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.3">Psa 63:3</reference>) נעם ה (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">Psa 90:17</reference>), the pleasantness (or gracefulness) of Jahve, i.e., His revelation, full of grace, which is there visible to the eye of the spirit. The interpretation which regards <hi type="italic">amaenitas</hi> as being equivalent to <hi type="italic">amaenus cultus</hi> takes hold of the idea from the wrong side. The assertion that בּקּר בּ is intended as a synonym of חזה בּ, of a pleased and lingering contemplation (Hupf., Hitz.), is contrary to the meaning of the verb, which signifies “to examine (with ל to seek or spie about after anything, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.36">Lev 13:36</reference>), to reflect on, or consider;” even the post-biblical signification to visit, more especially the sick (whence בּקּוּר הלים), comes from the primary meaning <hi type="italic">investigare</hi>. An appropriate sense may be obtained in the present instance by regarding it as a denominative from בּקשׁ and rendering it as Dunash and Rashi have done, “and to appear early in His temple;” but it is unnecessary to depart from the general usage of the language. Hengstenberg rightly retains the signification “to meditate on.” בּהיכלו is a designation of the place consecrated to devotion, and לבקּר is meant to refer to contemplative meditation that loses itself in God who is there manifest. In <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference> David bases the justification of his desire upon that which the sanctuary of God is to him; the futures affirm what Jahve will provide for him in His sanctuary. It is a refuge in which he may hide himself, where Jahve takes good care of him who takes refuge therein from the storms of trouble that rage outside: there he is far removed from all dangers, he is lifted high above them and his feet are upon rocky ground. The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> may be read בּסכּה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.21">Psa 31:21</reference> and with Ewald §257, <hi type="italic">d</hi>; but, in this passage, with אהל alternates סך, which takes the place of סכּה in the poetic style (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.3">Psa 76:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">Lam 2:6</reference>), though it does not do so by itself, but always with a suffix.<note placement="foot">Just in like manner they say in poetic style צידהּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.15">Psa 132:15</reference>; פּנּהּ, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.8">Pro 7:8</reference>; מדּה, <reference osisRef="Job.11.9">Job 11:9</reference>; גּלּהּ, Zec 4:2; and perhaps even נצּהּ, <reference osisRef="Gen.40.10">Gen 40:10</reference>; for צידתהּ, פּנּתהּ, מדּתהּ, גּלּתהּ, and נצּתהּ; as, in general, shorter forms are sometimes found in the inflexion, which do not occur in the corresponding principal form, e.g., צוּרם, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Psa 49:15</reference>, for צוּרתם; מגוּרם, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>, for מגוּרתם; בּערמם, <reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>, for בּערמתם; בּתבוּנם, Hos 13:2, for בּתבוּנתם; פּחם; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.14">Neh 5:14</reference>, for פּחתם; cf. Hitzig on Hos 13:2, and <hi type="italic">Böttcher’s Neue Aehrenlese,</hi> No. 693.</note>
entries.ba0c4a856c1a3ccd3d22a5f9840b6f636ea14df6: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">Psa 27:6</reference> <div eID="gen9335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9336" type="x-p"/> With ועתּה the poet predicts inferentially (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">Psa 2:10</reference>) the fulfilment of what he fervently desires, the guarantee of which lies in his very longing itself. זבחי תּרוּעה do not mean sacrifices in connection with which the trumpets are blown by the priests; for this was only the case in connection with the sacrifices of the whole congregation (Num 10:10), not with those of individuals. תּרוּעה is a synonym of תּודה, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.7">Psa 26:7</reference>; and זבחי תּרוּעה is a stronger form of expression for זבחי תודה (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.22">Psa 107:22</reference>), i.e., (cf. זבחי צדק, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>; 51:21) sacrifices of jubilant thanksgiving: he will offer sacrifices in which his gratitude plays a prominent part, and will sing songs of thanksgiving, accompanied by the playing of stringed instruments, to his Deliverer, who has again and so gloriously verified His promises.
entries.803bb4727d79774f632ae4f33aefaa8969755daf: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7-Ps.27.8">Psa 27:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen9336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9337" type="x-p"/> Vows of thanksgiving on the assumption of the answering of the prayer and the fulfilment of the thing supplicated, are very common at the close of Psalms. But in this Psalm the prayer is only just beginning at this stage. The transition is brought about by the preceding conception of the danger that threatens him from the side of his foes who are round about him. The reality, which, in the first part, is overcome and surmounted by his faith, makes itself consciously felt here. It is not to be rendered, as has been done by the Vulgate, <hi type="italic">Exaudi Domine vocem qua clamavi</hi> (rather, <hi type="italic">clamo</hi>) <hi type="italic">ad te</hi> (the introit of the <hi type="italic">Dominica exspectationis</hi> in the interval of preparation between Ascension and Pentecost). שׁמע has <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, and accordingly קולי אקרא, <hi type="italic">voce mea</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>) <hi type="italic">clamo</hi>, is an adverbial clause equivalent to <hi type="italic">voce mea clamante me</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Psa 27:8</reference> לך cannot possibly be so rendered that ל is treated as <hi type="italic">Lamed auctoris</hi> (Dathe, Olshausen): Thine, saith my heart, is (the utterance:) seek ye may face. The declaration is opposed to this sense, thus artificially put upon it. לך אמר are undoubtedly to be construed together; and what the heart says to Jahve is not: Seek ye my face, but by reason of this, and as its echo (Calvin: <hi type="italic">velut Deo succinens</hi>): I will therefore seek Thy face. Just as in <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>, a personal inference is drawn from a directly quoted saying of God. In the periodic style it would be necessary to transpose בּקּשׁוּ פּני thus: since Thou hast permitted and exhorted us, or in accordance with Thy persuasive invitation, that we should seek Thy face, I do seek Thy face (Hupfeld). There is no retrospective reference to any particular passage in the Tôra, such as Deu 4:29. The prayer is not based upon any single passage of Scripture, but upon God’s commands and promises in general.
entries.61b7cb31b39dd47432f7e2c7ead84b23e3a5af31: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9-Ps.27.10">Psa 27:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen9337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9338" type="x-p"/> The requests are now poured forth with all the greater freedom and importunity, that God may be willing to be entreated and invoked. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הטּה signifies in this passage standing by itself (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.24.4">Job 24:4</reference>): to push aside. The clause עזרתי היית does not say: be Thou my help (which is impossible on syntactical grounds), nor is it to be taken relatively: Thou who wast my help (for which there is no ground in what precedes); but on the contrary the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. gives the ground of the request that follows “Thou art my help (lit., Thou has become, or hast ever been) - cast me, then, not away,” and it is, moreover, accented accordingly. <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Psa 27:10</reference>, as we have already observed, does not sound as though it came from the lips of David, of whom it is only said during the time of his persecution by Saul, that at that time he was obliged to part from his parents, 1Sa 22:3. The words certainly might be David’s, if <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Psa 27:10</reference></hi> would admit of being taken hypothetically, as is done by Ewald, §362, <hi type="italic">b</hi>: should my father and my mother forsake me, yet Jahve will etc. But the entreaty “forsake me not” is naturally followed by the reason: for my father and my mother have forsaken me; and just as naturally does the consolation: but Jahve will take me up, prepare the way for the entreaties which begin anew in Psa 27:11. Whereas, if כי is taken hypothetically, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference> stands disconnectedly in the midst of the surrounding requests. On יאספני cf. Jos 20:4.
entries.3be54d91fec4d64bbfd0840bdbdee8c9371b69fb: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11-Ps.27.12">Psa 27:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen9338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9339" type="x-p"/> He is now wandering about like a hunted deer; but God is able to guide him so that he may escape all dangers. And this is what he prays for. As in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">Psa 143:10</reference>, מישׁור is used in an ethical sense; and differs in this respect from its use in Psa 26:12. On שׁררים, see the primary passage <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>, of which this is an echo. Wily spies dodge his every step and would gladly see what they have invented against him and wished for him, realised. Should he enter the way of sin leading to destruction, it would tend to the dishonour of God, just as on the contrary it is a matter of honour with God not to let His servant fall. Hence he prays to be led in the way of God, for a oneness of his own will with the divine renders a man inaccessible to evil. נפשׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">Psa 27:12</reference>, is used, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.9">Psa 17:9</reference>, and in the similar passage, which is genuinely Davidic, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.3">Psa 41:3</reference>, in the signification passion or strong desire; because the soul, in its natural state, is selfishness and inordinate desire. יפח is a collateral form of יפיח; they are both adjectives formed from the future of the verb פּוּח (like ירב, יריב): accustomed to breathe out (exhale), i.e., either to express, or to snort, breathe forth (cf. πνεῖν, or ἐμπνεῖν φόνον and θόνοῦ, θυμον, and the like, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.1">Act 9:1</reference>). In both Hitzig sees participles of יפח (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.31">Jer 4:31</reference>); but <reference osisRef="Ps.10.5">Psa 10:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab 2:3</reference> lead back to פּוּח (פּיח); and Hupfeld rightly recognises such nouns formed from futures to be, according to their original source, circumlocutions of the participle after the manner of an elliptical relative clause (the <hi type="italic">ṣifat</hi> of the Arabic syntax), and explains יפיח כּזבים, together with יפח חמס, from the verbal construction which still continues in force.
entries.e46f0b186fe33ce65068c3dc5ef5939d01205ce7: <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13-Ps.27.14">Psa 27:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen9339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9340" type="x-p"/> Self-encouragement to firmer confidence of faith. Joined to <reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">Psa 27:12</reference> (Aben-Ezra, Kimchi), <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference> trails badly after it. We must, with Geier, Dachselt, and others, suppose that the apodosis is wanting to the protasis with its לוּלא pointed with three points above,<note placement="foot">The ו has not any point above it, because it might be easily mistaken for a <hi type="italic">Cholem</hi>, vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi> p. 130.</note> and four below, according to the Masora (cf. <hi type="italic">B. Berachoth</hi> 4 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), but a word which is indispensably necessary, and is even attested by the lxx (ἑαυτῇ) and the Targum (although not by any other of the ancient versions); cf. the protasis with לוּ, which has no apodosis, in <reference osisRef="Gen.50.15">Gen 50:15</reference>, and the apodoses with כּי after לוּלי in <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen 31:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.10">Gen 43:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.1">1</reference> Sam. 35:34; <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.27">2Sa 2:27</reference> (also Num 22:33, where אוּלי = אם לא = לוּלי), which are likewise to be explained <hi type="italic">per aposiopesin</hi>. The perfect after לוּלא (לוּלי) has sometimes the sense of a <hi type="italic">plusquamperfectum</hi> (as in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.10">Gen 43:10</reference>, <hi type="italic">nisi cunctati essemus</hi>), and sometimes the sense of an <hi type="italic">imperfect</hi>, as in the present passage (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">Deu 32:29</reference> <hi type="italic">, si saperent</hi>). The poet does not speak of a faith that he once had, a past faith, but, in regard to the danger that is even now abiding and present, of the faith he now has, a present faith. The apodosis ought to run something like this (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.92">Psa 119:92</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.17">Psa 94:17</reference>): did I not believe, were not confidence preserved to me...then (אז( ne or כּי אז) I should perish; or: then I had suddenly perished. But he has such faith, and he accordingly in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">Psa 27:14</reference> encourages himself to go on cheerfully waiting and hoping; he speaks to himself, it is, as it were, the believing half of his soul addressing the despondent and weaker half. Instead of ואמץ (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.7">Deu 31:7</reference>) the expression is, as in Ps 31:25, ויאמץ לבּך, let thy heart be strong, let it give proof of strength. The rendering “May He (Jahve) strengthen thy heart” would require יאמּץ; but האמיץ, as e.g., הרחיב <reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">Psa 25:17</reference>, belongs to the transitive denominatives applying to the mind or spirit, in which the Hebrew is by no means poor, and in which the Arabic is especially rich.  <chapter eID="Ps.27"/> <div eID="gen9340" type="x-p"/>

entries.2206d578ea1516f778f7abaeab8510147ac9fb41:
PSALM 27.
In this psalm, David rehearses the desires and meditations with which he had exercised himself in the midst of his great dangers. The thanksgivings which he mingles with them show that it was composed after his deliverance. It is also probable that he repeats at once the prayers which had exercised his thoughts in his different meditations. Hence it is to be seen here with what invincible fortitude of soul the holy man was endued, that he might overcome the most grievous assaults of his enemies. His wonderful piety shines forth in this, that he wished to live for no other purpose than to serve God: nor could he be turned aside from this purpose by any anxiety or trouble.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 27:1-3
1. Jehovah is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? Jehovah is the strength of my life, of whom shall I be afraid? 2. When the wicked came upon me to eat up my flesh, when my oppressors and mine enemies came upon me, they stumbled and fell. 3. Though armies should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident.
 
1. Jehovah is my light. This commencement may be understood as meaning that David, having already experienced God’s mercy, publishes a testimony of his gratitude. But I rather incline to another meaning, namely, that, perceiving the conflict he had to wage with the sharpest temptations, he fortifies himself beforehand, and as it were brings together matter for confidence: for it is necessary that the saints earnestly wrestle with themselves to repel or subdue the doubts which the flesh is so prone to cherish, that they may cheerfully and speedily betake themselves to prayer. David, accordingly, having been tossed with various tempests, at length recovers himself, and shouts triumphantly over the troubles with which he had been harassed, rejoicing that whenever God displays his mercy and favor, there is nothing to be feared. This is farther intimated by the accumulation of terms which he employs, when he calls God not only his light, but his salvation, and the rock or strength of his life His object was, to put a threefold shield, as it were, against his various fears, as sufficient to ward them off. The term light, as is well known, is used in Scripture to denote joy, or the perfection of happiness. Farther, to explain his meaning, he adds that God was his salvation and the strength of his life, as it was by his help that he felt himself safe, and free from the terrors of death. Certainly we find that all our fears arise from this source, that we are too anxious about our life, while we acknowledge not that God is its preserver. We can have no tranquillity, therefore, until we attain the persuasion that our life is sufficiently guarded, because it is protected by his omnipotent power. The interrogation, too, shows how highly David esteemed the Divine protection, as he thus boldly exults against all his enemies and dangers. Nor assuredly do we ascribe due homage to God, unless, trusting to his promised aid, we dare to boast of the certainty of our safety. Weighing, as it were, in scales the whole power of earth and hell, David accounts it all lighter than a feather, and considers God alone as far outweighing the whole.
Let us learn, therefore, to put such a value on God’s power to protect us as to put to flight all our fears. Not that the minds of the faithful can, by reason of the infirmity of the flesh, be at all times entirely devoid of fear; but immediately recovering courage, let us, from the high tower of our confidence, look down upon all our dangers with contempt. Those who have never tasted the grace of God tremble because they refuse to rely on him, and imagine that he is often incensed against them, or at least far removed from them. But with the promises of God before our eyes, and the grace which they offer, our unbelief does him grievous wrong, if we do not with unshrinking courage boldly set him against all our enemies. When God, therefore, kindly allures us to himself, and assures us that he will take care of our safety, since we have embraced his promises, or because we believe him to be faithful, it is meet that we highly extol his power, that it may ravish our hearts with admiration of himself. We must mark well this comparison, What are all creatures to God? Moreover, we must extend this confidence still farther, in order to banish all fears from our consciences, like Paul, who, when speaking of his eternal salvation, boldly exclaims,
“If God be for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:34.)
